mainTopic: The storekeeper's liability and שואל שלא מדעת; when a buyer who picks up merchandise becomes responsible for it or owns it; the new משנה on cleaning measures
overview: The amud opens with the storekeeper (חנווני) from the משנה, who is liable for a child's broken jug even after handing it back. The first answer, that he picked up the jug to measure, like רבה's rule about a lost animal, is rejected. רבא, together with רבי זירא, explains instead that the storekeeper used the jug to measure for other customers. So חכמים and רבי יהודה disagree about שואל שלא מדעת: is he a regular borrower or a גזלן? The גמרא then turns to שמואל's rule that someone who takes a vessel to examine it pays even for an אונס, but only when the price is fixed. Two stories apply this rule: meat snatched by a horseman, and pumpkins that the seller tried to make הקדש. A ברייתא then teaches that a buyer who decides in his heart to buy vegetables owns them and must tithe them, and רב הושעיא limits this to a ירא שמים like רב ספרא. The amud ends with a new משנה on how often sellers must clean their measures, weights and scales.

steps.title: Taking the jug to measure makes him responsible, like רבה's rule
steps.stepSummary: The storekeeper is liable because he took the jug into his hands to measure with it. This is compared to רבה's rule that hitting a lost animal to lead it makes you obligated to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where the storekeeper took the jug to measure with it. This follows רבה, who said: if he hit the animal to lead it, he became obligated for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why the storekeeper is still liable after handing the jug back. It says he picked up the jug to measure with it, and it brings support from a rule of רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By picking up the jug, the storekeeper actively took charge of it. רבה taught that a finder who was not obligated to return a lost animal becomes obligated once he hits it to lead it. The idea is that physically getting involved with the object makes you responsible for it.

keyTerms.meaning: For example; the case is where…
He struck it (to lead the animal along)

phrases.english: For example, where he took it to measure with it,
phrases.notes: "He" is the storekeeper, and "it" is the child's jug.

phrases.english: and this follows רבה, for רבה said:
If he struck it, he became obligated for it.
phrases.notes: רבה is talking about finding a lost animal. Once you hit it to lead it along, you must return it to its owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier question, which comes before this section: why is the storekeeper liable if he already returned the jug to the child?
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case narrowly and supports it with an outside ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Handing the jug back to the child should end the storekeeper's responsibility.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because he took the jug into his hands to measure, he took responsibility for it, like רבה's rule.

steps.title: The comparison to רבה does not fit a jug
steps.stepSummary: רבה's rule applies to animals, because hitting them trains them to wander off. Picking up a jug does not make anything worse.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can say רבה said his rule about animals, because the finder got them used to stepping outside. But in a case like this one, did he say it?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the comparison from step 1. It argues that רבה's rule was based on something special about animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the finder hits an animal, he teaches it to stray, so he has actually made things worse for the owner. That is why he becomes responsible. A storekeeper who picks up a jug to measure with it does nothing to make the jug more likely to break, so the reason behind רבה's rule does not apply here.

phrases.english: Say that רבה said it about animals,
because he taught them to take steps outside;
phrases.notes: He means that hitting the animals got them used to wandering away, so the finder made the owner's situation worse.

phrases.english: but in a case like this, did he say it?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support from רבה that step 1 relied on.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison to רבה, and with it the first answer to why the storekeeper is liable.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבה's rule depends on the finder making things worse by teaching the animal to stray. Picking up a jug does no such harm.

steps.title: רבא and רבי זירא: he measured for other customers
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a new answer that he worked out with רבי זירא. The storekeeper used the child's jug to measure for other people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: I and the lion of the group explained it. And who is that? רבי זירא. Here we are dealing with a case where the storekeeper took the jug to measure with it for others.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first answer was rejected, רבא offers a fresh explanation of the משנה. He sets up a new case: the storekeeper used the jug for other customers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new case is not about touching the jug. It is about using someone else's jug for his own business without the father's permission. That turns the storekeeper into someone who borrowed the jug without the owner knowing, and the next step builds on this.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the earlier answer and starts a new one)
The lion of the group, a title for the greatest scholar among them
What case are we dealing with here?

phrases.english: I and the lion of the group explained it:
phrases.notes: "Lion" is a nickname of honor for the strongest scholar in the study group.

phrases.english: And who is he? רבי זירא;
What are we dealing with here?
A case where he took it to measure with it for others.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: אֲנִי וַאֲרִי שֶׁבַּחֲבוּרָה תַּרְגֵּימְנוּהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer that step 2 rejected with a new way of setting up the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The storekeeper's liability came from simply picking up the jug, like רבה's rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The storekeeper used the jug for other customers without permission, and that use is what makes him responsible.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רבה (step 1) and רבא (this step). They are two different אמוראים with almost the same name.

steps.title: The dispute is about borrowing without permission
steps.stepSummary: חכמים and רבי יהודה disagree about שואל שלא מדעת. One holds he is a regular borrower, and the other holds he is a robber (גזלן).
steps.simpleTranslation: They disagree about someone who borrows without the owner knowing. One Sage holds he is a borrower, and the other Sage holds he is a robber.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבא's answer. It explains that the disagreement in the משנה is really about how to treat someone who borrows without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A regular borrower can return the item to the place where he got it, so handing it back to the child is enough, and the storekeeper is exempt. That is רבי יהודה's view. A robber must return the item to the owner himself, so the storekeeper stays responsible until the jug reaches the father. That is the view of חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who borrows without the owner's knowledge

phrases.english: And they disagree about one who borrows without the owner's knowledge:
One Sage holds: he is a borrower,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהודה, who exempts the storekeeper.

phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: he is a robber.
phrases.notes: This is חכמים, who make the storekeeper pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's answer by showing what the dispute in the משנה is about.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the underlying reason for the dispute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It was not clear what principle the dispute between חכמים and רבי יהודה depends on.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute depends on whether someone who borrows without permission is a regular borrower (exempt once he gives the item back) or a robber (liable until the item reaches the owner).
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, the storekeeper used the child's jug for his own customers without the father's permission. רבי יהודה treats him like a regular borrower, so giving the jug back to the child ends his responsibility. חכמים treat him like a גזלן, who stays liable until the jug gets back to its owner.
steps.whyThisMatters: שואל שלא מדעת is a basic idea that comes up in many places in ש״ס. This case shows the practical result: does returning the item to where you took it from end your responsibility, or must it reach the owner himself?

steps.title: שמואל: taking a vessel to examine it makes you liable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to שמואל's ruling. Someone who takes a vessel from a craftsman to look it over is liable if an accident happens to it while he holds it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the main statement. שמואל said: if someone takes a vessel from a craftsman to examine it, and an accident happens to it while it is in his hands, he must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to look closely at שמואל's ruling, which it mentioned earlier. It now quotes the ruling in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you only pay for an אונס (an accident you could not prevent) if the item is fully your responsibility. שמואל says a person examining an item before buying it already carries that responsibility. The next line will explain when this is true.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The matter itself': the גמרא returns to examine a statement it quoted earlier
A craftsman who makes and sells vessels
To examine it, to check it before buying
An accident beyond his control happened (אוֹנֶס)

phrases.english: One who takes a vessel from a craftsman
and an accident happened while it was in his hand

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the storekeeper discussion and returns to examine שמואל's ruling directly.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who takes a craftsman's vessel to examine it is liable even for an accident while it is in his hands.

steps.title: Limit: only when the price is already fixed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits שמואל's ruling to a case where the price of the vessel is already set.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this rule applies only when the price of the item is fixed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a condition to שמואל's rule: it only applies when the price is already settled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the price is fixed, nothing is left to bargain over. If the buyer finds nothing wrong, he will buy it, so his picking it up already counts as mostly a sale. If the price was still open, the item stays the seller's responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And these words apply': this rule is limited to the following case
Its price is fixed and settled

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think simply touching an item makes you its owner. This only works when the price is fixed, so the sale is really already decided.

phrases.english: only where its price is fixed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the case where שמואל's ruling applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל's liability applies only when the item's price is fixed.

steps.title: The meat snatched by a horseman: רב יימר makes the buyer pay
steps.stepSummary: A man lifted a piece of meat in a butcher shop, and a horseman snatched it from him. רב יימר ruled that the man must pay the butcher, but only where the price is fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man went into a butcher shop and lifted a thigh of meat. While he was lifting it, a horseman came and grabbed it from him. The case came before רב יימר, who made him pay for it. And this applies only when the price is fixed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case that follows the same idea as שמואל. The buyer must pay for meat that was snatched from him by force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being robbed by a horseman is a clear אונס, yet the buyer still pays, just like in שמואל's case. Because the price was fixed, lifting the meat already made it the buyer's responsibility. The גמרא repeats the fixed-price condition to show it applies here too.

keyTerms.meaning: A horseman, a mounted soldier or robber

phrases.english: A certain man entered a butcher shop,
and lifted a thigh of meat.
a horseman came and snatched it from him.
who obligated him to pay its value.
only where its price is fixed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real ruling that follows שמואל's principle and repeats the fixed-price condition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer who lifts meat with a fixed price must pay if it is snatched from him.

steps.title: The pumpkin seller declares his pumpkins הקדש
steps.stepSummary: A man brought pumpkins to פום נהרא. Everyone took one, and the seller declared them all הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man brought pumpkins to פום נהרא. Everyone came and each took a pumpkin. He said to them: they are hereby consecrated to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story to set up the next ruling. It has not given a ruling yet; that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers took the pumpkins but had not paid. The seller then tried to make them הקדש. The question is whether the pumpkins were still his, so that his declaration could work.

keyTerms.meaning: פום נהרא, a town in בבל

phrases.english: They are hereby consecrated to Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאַיְיתִי קָארֵי לְפוּם נַהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a third case to test the same principle, this time for הקדש instead of liability.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: the seller declared already-taken pumpkins הקדש.

steps.title: רב כהנא: you cannot consecrate what is no longer yours, unless the price was open
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא rules that the הקדש does not work, because the pumpkins already belonged to the buyers. This is true only if the price was fixed. If it was not fixed, they were still the seller's, and his הקדש works.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came before רב כהנא. He told them: a person cannot consecrate something that is not his. And this applies only when the price is fixed. But if the price is not fixed, the pumpkins are still in their owner's possession, and he consecrated them properly.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא decides the pumpkin case. Then the גמרא spells out both sides: with a fixed price the הקדש fails, and with an open price it works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a fixed price, taking the item already makes it the buyer's, so the seller no longer owns it and cannot make it הקדש. With an open price, no sale has happened yet, so the item is still the seller's and his הקדש takes effect. The same fixed-price rule decides liability and ownership.

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם מַקְדִּישׁ דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A person cannot consecrate something that does not belong to him
In the possession of their owner
He consecrated it properly, and it took effect

steps.whatToRemember: Picking up an item to buy it counts as taking it over only when the price is fixed (קייצי דמיה). Then the buyer pays even for an אונס, and the seller can no longer make it הקדש. If the price is open, the item still belongs to the seller.
steps.whyThisMatters: The fixed-price condition is repeated three times, which shows it is the key to the whole section. Whether the sale is already decided controls both who pays for accidents and who owns the item.

phrases.english: only where their price is fixed,
but if their price is not fixed
they remain in their owner's possession,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the pumpkin case from step 8 and applies the fixed-price condition in both directions.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When the price is fixed, taking an item transfers it to the buyer, so the seller cannot make it הקדש. When the price is open, it stays the seller's and his הקדש works.

steps.title: Picking out vegetables does not make you the owner
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a buyer who sorts and sets aside vegetables, even all day, has not acquired them and is not obligated in מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who buys vegetables in the market, and sorts them and sets some aside, even all day long, has not acquired them and is not obligated to separate מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a shopper who sorts vegetables at a stall. Just choosing them does not make them his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the theme of the earlier steps: when does a buyer become the owner of something he is holding? Here, sorting and setting aside is only looking. No decision has been made, so nothing has changed hands.

keyTerms.meaning: Tithe, a portion of produce that must be separated

phrases.english: One who buys vegetables from the market,
and has not become obligated in מעשר.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַלּוֹקֵחַ יָרָק מִן הַשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא on the same theme as the earlier cases: when a buyer who is holding merchandise becomes its owner.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sorting and setting aside vegetables, without deciding to buy, does not acquire them and does not create a מעשר obligation.

steps.title: Deciding to buy makes him the owner, which creates a problem
steps.stepSummary: Once he decides in his heart to buy, he owns the vegetables and must tithe them. Now he can't simply return them, and he can't tithe and return them either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he decided in his heart to buy it, he acquired it and became obligated in מעשר. He cannot return it, since it is already obligated in מעשר. He cannot tithe it and return it, since that would lower its value.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues: once the buyer decides to buy, the vegetables are his and need tithing. It then lays out a problem if he wants to back out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decision itself is the turning point that makes him the owner. Returning untithed produce is not allowed, because it is already obligated. Tithing it and then giving it back would leave the seller with less produce than he gave.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'decided in his heart' as a formal קנין. He did no act of acquisition at all. The גמרא will soon ask exactly how a thought can work.

phrases.english: If he decided in his heart to buy it,
he acquired it and became obligated in מעשר.
since it has already become obligated in מעשר,
and to tithe it is impossible,
phrases.notes: Meaning: to tithe it and then hand it back to the seller.

phrases.english: since he would then be lowering their value.

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּמַר בְּלִבּוֹ לִקְנוֹתוֹ – קָנָה וְנִתְחַיֵּיב בְּמַעֲשֵׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case of step 10: here the buyer did decide to buy, and the ברייתא lays out the problem this creates.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A firm decision to buy acquires the produce and obligates it in מעשר, so it can no longer be returned either untithed or tithed.

steps.title: The solution: tithe it and pay for the tithe
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא solves the problem. The buyer tithes the produce and pays the seller the value of the tithe portion.
steps.simpleTranslation: So how should he act? He tithes it and gives the seller the money for the tithe.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question of what the buyer should do now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tithing takes care of the מעשר obligation. Paying for the tithe portion makes sure the seller does not lose money. This solves both sides of the problem from step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: The money value of the tithe portion

steps.whatToRemember: Once a buyer decides to buy, he owns the produce and must tithe it. If he wants to back out, he tithes it and pays the seller for the portion taken as מעשר.

phrases.english: and gives him the money for the מעשר.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the seller, who is paid for the part that was taken off as tithe.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד? מְעַשְּׂרוֹ, וְנוֹתֵן לוֹ דְּמֵי מַעֲשֵׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the problem raised in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He separates מעשר and pays the seller the value of the tithe portion.

steps.title: How can a mere thought make someone the owner?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: just deciding in one's heart, with no act or words, should not acquire anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that because he decided in his heart to buy, he acquired it and became obligated in מעשר?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא. A purchase normally needs an action, so a silent decision should not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ownership normally passes through a קנין, which is a physical act like lifting or pulling. The ברייתא seems to let a private thought do the job. That clashes with basic rules of acquisition.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (a surprised challenge)

phrases.english: Is that to say that because he decided in his heart to buy,
he acquired it and became obligated in מעשר?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling of step 11 that a decision of the heart acquires.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that גמר בלבו לקנותו – קנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Acquisition requires an act or a formal קנין. A thought alone should not move ownership or create a מעשר obligation.

steps.title: The case is a ירא שמים like רב ספרא
steps.stepSummary: רב הושעיא explains that the ברייתא is talking about a ירא שמים who holds himself bound by his inner decisions, like רב ספרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הושעיא said: Here we are dealing with a God-fearing person, like רב ספרא, who lived by the verse 'and speaks truth in his heart.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב הושעיא answers the challenge by narrowing the case to a very honest person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For an ordinary person, a thought does not acquire. But a person like רב ספרא treats his inner decision as binding, as if he had said it out loud. For such a person, the moment he decides is the moment the purchase is final for him.

keyTerms.meaning: And speaks truth in his heart (keeps even his unspoken commitments)

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's rule that a decision of the heart acquires applies only to a person on the level of רב ספרא, who keeps even his silent commitments.

phrases.english: Here we are dealing with a God-fearing person,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא: הָכָא בִּירֵא שָׁמַיִם עָסְקִינַן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא) to a special type of person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say that any buyer acquires through a mere thought.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a ירא שמים who treats his inner decisions as binding, like רב ספרא, is considered to have bought at the moment he decides.

steps.title: New משנה: how often sellers must clean their measures
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a סיטון must clean his measuring vessels every thirty days, and a בעל הבית once every twelve months.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A wholesaler wipes clean his measures once every thirty days. A homeowner does so once every twelve months.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about honesty in measuring. It tells sellers how often to clean leftover residue from their measuring vessels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leftover liquid sticks inside the measure and makes it hold less, which cheats the buyer. The first opinion requires the busy wholesaler to clean more often than a homeowner who sells only now and then.

phrases.english: The wholesaler wipes clean his measures

steps.triggerLanguage: הַסִּיטוֹן מְקַנֵּחַ מִדּוֹתָיו אֶחָד לִשְׁלשִׁים יוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה on honest measures, after the discussion of when a sale takes effect.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סיטון cleans his measures every thirty days; a בעל הבית every twelve months.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל reverses the rule
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds the opposite: the homeowner must clean more often, and the wholesaler less often.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: The matters are reversed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees with the first opinion of the משנה and flips the two time periods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His reasoning is that constant use keeps residue from sticking, so the wholesaler's measures stay clean. A homeowner's measures sit unused, the residue hardens, and so they need cleaning every thirty days.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the first opinion

steps.confusionAlert: 'Reversed' means the time periods switch: the בעל הבית cleans every thirty days, and the סיטון once a year.
steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: חִילּוּף הַדְּבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the first opinion of the משנה in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The סיטון cleans once every twelve months, and the בעל הבית every thirty days.

steps.title: How often a storekeeper must clean his measures, weights and scales
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a חנווני cleans his measuring vessels twice a week, wipes his weights once a week, and cleans his scales after every single weighing.
steps.simpleTranslation: A storekeeper cleans his measuring vessels twice a week, wipes his weights once a week, and cleans his scales after each and every weighing.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a third kind of seller, the small storekeeper, and tells us how often he must clean each of his tools.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סיטון cleans every thirty days and a בעל הבית every twelve months, but the חנווני sells small amounts all day, so leftover stuff builds up fast. That is why he cleans much more often. Each tool gets its own schedule: measures twice a week, weights once a week, and the scale pans after every weighing.

keyTerms.meaning: A small storekeeper who sells in small amounts

phrases.english: A storekeeper cleans his measuring vessels

phrases.notes: Here שַׁבָּת means a week, not the day of שבת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of cleaning schedules, adding the storekeeper after the סיטון and the בעל הבית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חנווני cleans his measures twice a week, his weights once a week, and his scales after every weighing.

steps.title: The cleaning rule applies only to moist goods
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל limits the cleaning rule: it applies to moist goods, but with dry goods there is no need to clean.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said: When is this said? With moist goods. But with dry goods, he does not need to clean.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל sets a limit on the cleaning rules we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason for cleaning is that leftover stuff sticks to the tools and makes the next measure come out short for the customer. Moist goods (like oil or wine) stick, so cleaning is needed. Dry goods do not stick, so there is nothing to clean.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case are these words said? (introduces a limit on a rule)

steps.whatToRemember: Cleaning measures is about stopping hidden cheating from leftover stuff. Busier sellers clean more often, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the rule applies only to moist goods that stick.

phrases.english: In what case are these words said?
but with dry goods, he does not need to.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the cleaning rules just stated, saying they apply only to moist goods.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cleaning measuring tools is required only for moist goods. Dry goods do not require it.
